open_obligations: Check whether debate variants with judge interaction or abstention remain zero-sum.
Note Chen et al.'s own limitation that general-sum language games are unstudied.
Check that LLM debaters' outputs fit Chen et al.'s finite-action game model.
in.other_title: Debate modelled as a zero-sum game, so external regret minimization suffices
in.rationale: Irving et al. define debate as a zero-sum game where each agent maximises its probability of winning. Chen et al. state AI Safety via Debate is predominantly captured by zero-sum games, where coarse correlated and correlated equilibria are Nash equilibria, so the game can be played efficiently by minimising external regret.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: modelling AI debate as a zero-sum game so that external-regret minimisation suffices

open_obligations: Check that the doubly-efficient protocols' payoffs are zero-sum as in Irving et al.
Note that inference-time trust in A depends on B being a capable opponent.
Check how many human verifier queries training actually needs.
in.other_title: Training and inference with debate: human labels needed only for verifier queries
in.rationale: Irving et al. define debate as a zero-sum game in which each agent maximises its probability of winning. Brown-Cohen et al.'s training mapping has pretrained debaters trained by self-play on the zero-sum debate game, with human labels only for verifier queries, and trusts A's output at inference unless B aborts or points out a flaw; this relies on the zero-sum game structure.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: training debaters by self-play on a zero-sum debate game and trusting the winner's output

open_obligations: Check whether judge-ended debates preserve the zero-sum structure Irving et al. assume.
Note that Michael et al.'s debaters are often humans, not self-play agents.
Check that certified quotes do not make the judge's task trivially verifiable.
in.other_title: Information-asymmetric interactive debate with certified quotes and judge-ended rounds
in.rationale: Irving et al. define a debate game where two agents state answers, alternate statements and a judge picks the winner. Michael et al. define an information-asymmetric debate where the judge states prior credences, interjects between turns, ends the debate when ready, and debaters can include certified verbatim quotes up to l_q characters per turn; these additions change the game from fixed alternation to judge-controlled interaction.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: two-debater debate protocols judged by a weaker party, extended with judge interaction and certified evidence

open_obligations: Check whether the prover-verifier game is presented anywhere else in the paper as derived from debate, or only contrasted with it here

in.other_title: Anil et al. recast Irving et al.'s two-debater game as a one-prover game aimed at learning proof protocols
in.rationale: The authors position their game relative to Irving et al.'s debate game and state what they change (one prover instead of two debaters, learning a verification protocol as the goal), which is the closest fit to EXTENDS. The passage is in related work and does not claim agreement or conflict with debate results.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Game-theoretic set-ups in which a weak judge or verifier checks a stronger agent's messages; holds as a design relation, not a comparison of results

in.other_title: Michael et al. build on Irving et al.'s debate: assigned answers, judge interaction, softer lie rule
in.rationale: The passage explicitly says the approach builds on Irving et al. and lists the changes, which is the definition of EXTENDS. The third change is justified by debaters not being optimal, a departure from Irving et al.'s optimal-play analysis.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Debate protocol design; the changes are made for information-asymmetric reading comprehension with non-optimal human debaters

in.rationale: The passage names Irving et al.'s protocol and states the change the authors make (judging the full transcript rather than a single sub-component) while keeping the two-debater-plus-judge game, which fits EXTENDS.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Debate protocol design: full-transcript judging versus Irving et al.'s stricter sub-component judging; holds for short reading-comprehension debates

text: The authors define the simplest debate game: a question is shown to two agents, each states an answer (the answers may be the same), the agents alternate statements s0 to s(n-1), and the judge sees the question, answers and statements and decides which agent wins. The game is zero-sum, with each agent maximising its probability of winning.
title: Definition of the two-agent debate game (answers, alternating statements, judge)
